en: In the Mahāyāna, the triple world is established as representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), based on the sūtra which states:
"O sons of the Conqueror, the triple world is mind-only (*cittamātra*).
Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and representation (*vijñapti*) are synonyms.
Here, "mind" (citta) is intended to include its associated mental factors (saṃprayoga).
The word "only" (mātra) is for the purpose of negating external objects;
that is, this is representation-only (vijñaptimātra), because there is the appearance of non-existent objects.
Just as one suffering from ophthalmia sees non-existent things such as clusters of hair and the like. // 1 //
Here it is objected:
there is no such thing as an object;
there is neither a restriction of place and time, nor a lack of restriction regarding the mental continuum.
Furthermore, if representation does not exist as an object, its causal efficiency is not tenable. (2)
What is meant by this?
If the cognition of form and so forth arises without an object such as form, and not from an object such as form,
why does it arise in a particular location and not everywhere?
And it arises only in that specific place, not at all times;
for those established in that particular place and time, the arising occurs within the mental continua (*saṃtāna*) of all of them, not of just one alone—
just as the appearance of hair and so forth occurs in the continuum of those with cataracts, but not for others.
Why is it that the hair, bees, and so forth seen by those with ophthalmia do not perform the functions of hair and so on, yet they are not non-functional for others?

Why is it that the food, drink, clothing, poison, weapons, and so forth seen in a dream do not perform the functions of food and so on, yet they are not non-functional for others? And why is it that because a city of Gandharvas lacks substantial reality, it does not perform the functions of a city, yet it is not non-functional for others?

Therefore, regarding the manifestation of what is non-existent, the restriction of place and time, the lack of restriction to a [specific] continuum, and causal efficiency would not be tenable. Yet, they are indeed tenable; for:
"The restriction of place and so forth is established, as in a dream."
"Like a dream" means as in a dream. How so?
In a dream, even without an external object, bees, gardens, women, men, and so forth are seen in a particular place and not everywhere.
Furthermore, because it is seen in that very same place at certain times but not at all times, the restriction of place and time is established even in the absence of an external object;
moreover, as in the case of hungry ghosts,
there is no restriction regarding the mental continuum.
The term "accomplished" (siddha) carries over [from the previous context].
"Like hungry ghosts" means as with hungry ghosts.
How is it accomplished equally?
When everyone perceives a river of pus and so forth. // 3 //
The river filled with pus is the "Pus River" (*pūyanadī*), like the term "ghee-pot" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*).
For all hungry ghosts (*preta*), being in an identical state of the maturation of their karma (*karmavipāka*), see the river filled with pus; it is not only one individual who sees it.

Just as [it was described] as being filled with pus, so too by the use of the term "etc. it is understood to be filled with urine, excrement, and so forth, and to be presided over by men bearing clubs and swords;
thus, even in the absence of an external object, the lack of restriction regarding the continuity of cognitions is established.
It should be understood that the accomplishment of purposeful action is like a nocturnal emission;
just as in a dream there occurs a nocturnal emission characterized by the discharge of semen even without the union of a couple.
Thus, by means of various other examples, the fourfold set beginning with the restriction of place and time is established;
furthermore, it is like the case of the hells: everything [is established].
It should be understood that "siddham" means "like in the hells," that is, as in the case of the hells. How is it established?
In the perception of hell-guardians and the like, and in being oppressed by them; (4)

For just as in the hells, the seeing of hell-guardians and so forth by the denizens of hell is established through the restriction of place and time— as indicated by the phrase "and so forth," which includes the seeing of dogs, crows, iron mountains, and their coming and going— and this is established for all of them, not for just one alone, and by means of those guardians they inflict suffering upon them, even though the hell-guardians and such do not exist, due to the sovereign power of the common ripening of their own karma.
Likewise, it should be understood that elsewhere as well, this entire tetrad—beginning with the restriction of place and time—is established.
But what is the reason that those hell-wardens, as well as those dogs and crows, are not accepted as sentient beings?
Because it is illogical; for it is not tenable that they are hell-beings.
Likewise, because they would not experience that suffering,
there would be no established distinction between "these are the hell-beings" and "these are the hell-wardens" as they torment one another.
Furthermore, for those who are equal in form, size, and strength, there would be no such fear when tormenting one another.
Furthermore, being unable to endure the suffering of burning on a ground made of blazing iron, how could they torment others there?
Moreover, how could those who are not hell-beings possibly arise in hell?
At any rate, how could animals possibly be born in heaven?
In this way, there might be the existence of specific types of hell-beings, such as the hell-wardens and others, within the hells.

However, the birth of animals in heaven does not occur in the same way as it does in hell; nor is there the birth of hungry ghosts [there], because they do not experience the suffering born of that place. (5)

For those animals that are born in heaven do so by virtue of karma conducive to the happiness of that receptacle-world (bhājanaloka), and having been born there, they experience the pleasure arising from it.
However, the hell-wardens and others do not experience the suffering of hell;
therefore, the birth of animals there is not logical, nor is that of hungry ghosts (pretas).

In that case, by the karma of those hell-beings, specific types of primary elements arise there, distinguished by color, shape, size, and strength, which receive the designations "hell-guardians" and so forth;
and they transform accordingly.
That which is seen as performing two kinds of actions, such as the movement of hands and so forth, for the purpose of instilling fear—
just as mountains in the shape of rams are seen coming and going, and in the forest of iron *śālmalī* trees, the thorns are seen turning downward and upward—
that is not the case that they do not exist at all.
If it is accepted that, through those karmas, there is likewise the arising and transformation of the elements (bhūtas) therein, why is this not also accepted for consciousness? (6)
Why is it not accepted that consciousness itself undergoes such a transformation through those actions? Why, then, are the primary elements postulated?
Moreover:

Why is it that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an action is conceived as being in one place while its fruit is conceived as being in another? Why is it not accepted that [the fruit] occurs in the very same place where the impression resides? (7)

For by whatever karma such an arising and transformation of the primary elements (*bhūta*) for hell-beings there is postulated, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that karma is situated within their own stream of consciousness (*vijñāna-santāna*) and nowhere else.
Why, then, is it not accepted that its fruit—such a transformation of consciousness—occurs precisely where the impression is located?
What is the reason for imagining its fruit to be where the impression does not exist?
Scripture is the authority.

If consciousness alone were to appear as form and so forth, and there were no external object such as form, then the Blessed One would not have spoken of the existence of the sense-bases (āyatana) of form and so forth.
This [objection] is without foundation, because:
The existence of the sense-bases such as form was spoken with a specific intention toward those people who were to be trained, just like [the teaching on] spontaneously born beings. (8)

Just as the Blessed One stated, "There is a spontaneously born being," this was said by virtue of his underlying intention, referring to the non-interruption of the continuum of consciousness in the future;
for he also said, "There is no being here, nor a self; rather, these are phenomena accompanied by causes."

In this way, the existence of the sense-bases such as form was also spoken of by the Blessed One with reference to those persons to be trained by that teaching; therefore, that statement is intentional (ābhiprāyika).
What is the intended meaning here?
"Since a representation arises from its own seed with a certain appearance, the Sage spoke of those two as its twofold sense-base. (9)

What is meant by this? From whichever seed, having reached a specific transformation, a representation (vijñapti) appearing as form arises— the Blessed One has declared that seed and that appearance to be, respectively, the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) and the form-base (rūpa-āyatana) for that representation.

In this way, up to the representation appearing as the tangible: from whichever specific transformation of its own seed a representation arises, that seed and that appearance—the Blessed One has declared those two, respectively, to be the sense-fields of the body and the tangible for that [representation].
This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, what is the benefit of teaching in this way by means of intentional purpose?
It is for the sake of entering into the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*); for when it is taught in such a manner, they enter into the selflessness of the person.

The sixfold consciousness arises from a duality; there is no single seer, nor indeed any thinker. Having understood this, those who are to be trained through the teaching of the selflessness of persons enter into the selflessness of persons.
Otherwise, however...
The teaching is the entry into the selflessness of phenomena;
"otherwise" refers to the teaching of representation-only.
How is there entry into the selflessness of phenomena?

Having understood that this which arises as the appearance of phenomena such as form is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and that there is no phenomenon whatsoever possessing the characteristics of form and so forth;

if, then, no phenomenon exists in any way, does it not follow that even this "representation-only" does not exist? How, then, is it established? Indeed, the entry into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) does not occur by thinking that "no phenomenon exists in any way. Rather, [it is as follows:]
By means of its imagined nature. // 10 //

The intrinsic nature of phenomena, such as the grasped and the grasper, which is imagined by the foolish— by means of that imagined self, those phenomena are devoid of self (nairātmya), but not by way of the ineffable self that is the domain of the Buddhas. Thus, because one enters into the selflessness of even representation-only (vijñaptimātra) by means of the self imagined by another representation, there occurs the entry into the selflessness of all phenomena through the establishment of representation-only.
But this is not because of a denial of its existence;

for otherwise, one representation would have another representation as its object, and thus the state of being representation-only (*vijñaptimātratva*) would not be established, since representations would possess external objects.

But how is this to be understood: that the Blessed One spoke of the existence of the sense-bases such as form with this underlying intention, and not because those things which individually become the objects of the cognitions of form and so forth actually exist? Because:
"That object is neither one nor many when analyzed into atoms."
Nor are they composite, because the atom is not established. // 11 //
Thus it is said. What is meant?

That which is the sense-field (*āyatana*) consisting of form and so forth, which would be the respective object (*viṣaya*) of the cognitions of form and so forth, must be either a single entity—such as the "whole" (*avayavin*) postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas—or multiple, in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Or perhaps those very atoms are aggregated;

however, they cannot constitute a single object, because no form of a "whole" distinct from its parts is ever perceived anywhere. Nor can they constitute a plurality of objects, because [the individual] atoms... [are not so perceived].
Because they are not apprehended individually,
nor do they become objects when combined;
for this reason, the atom is not established as a single substance.
How is it not established? Because:
"Due to simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts.
When there is simultaneous conjunction with six atoms from six directions, it follows that the atom must possess six parts.
Because that which is the location of one cannot be the location of another,
and because the six [atoms] would occupy the same location, the aggregate would be no larger than a single atom. (12)
Now, that which is the location of one atom is the very same as that of six;

therefore, because they all occupy the same location, the entire aggregate would be no more than a single atom, since there is no mutual distinction between them. Consequently, no aggregate at all would be visible.
For atoms do not combine at all, because they lack parts;
lest this undesirable consequence should follow.
However, the Kashmiri Vaibhāṣikas maintain that when they are aggregated, they do combine with one another; these [Vaibhāṣikas] must be questioned as follows:
That which is an aggregate of atoms is not a separate entity from them;
since there is no conjunction of atoms, of what would that [conjunction] exist in their aggregate?
It is "conjunction" that is being discussed here.
Nor does its conjunction fail to be established on account of its being partless. // 13 //
Furthermore, if even aggregates do not join with one another,
then it should not be said that the conjunction of atoms is not established because they lack parts;
for even an aggregate, though possessing parts, is not admitted to have conjunction.
Therefore, an atom is not established as a single substance.
Whether the conjunction of atoms is accepted or not accepted,
that which possesses a distinction of spatial parts cannot logically be a unity.

For since the eastern part of an atom is distinct from its parts down to the downward part, when there is such a division of spatial directions (*digbhāga*), how can the unity of that atom—which consists of those parts—be tenable?
Or how could there be shadow and obstruction?
If each individual atom did not have a division of spatial directions, how could there be shadow in one place and sunlight in another when the sun rises?
For there is no other part of it where heat would not exist.
And how could there be an obstruction of one atom by another atom if a distinction of spatial parts (*digbhāgabheda*) is not admitted?
For there is no "other side" of an atom at all, such that, through its arrival there, one atom might be obstructed by another.

And since there would be no resistance [if atoms were not distinct], all composite objects would occupy the same location; thus it has been said that every aggregate would be merely the size of a single atom.
Why is it not accepted that the shadow and obstruction belong to the mass and not to the individual atom?
Is the mass indeed intended to be something other than the atoms, such that those two [conjunction and disjunction] could belong to it? No, he says:
"If the mass is not other [than the atoms], then those two do not belong to it. (14)
If the aggregate is not admitted to be something other than the atoms, it is established that "those [atoms] do not belong to it.
This is merely a conceptual construction of an arrangement, whether one calls it an "atom" or a "composite."
What is the point of this reflection if the characteristics,
such as form and so forth, are not refuted?
Furthermore, what is their characteristic?
It is the state of being an object of the eye and other [senses], as well as the state of being blue and so forth.
This very point is now to be deliberated: is that which is accepted as the object of the eye and other [senses]—namely, blue, yellow, and so on—a single substance, or rather, is it manifold?
And what follows from this? If there were multiplicity, the fault has already been stated;
if there were unity, there would be no gradual movement, nor the simultaneous occurrence of perception and non-perception.
Furthermore, there would be neither the occurrence of multiple discrete states nor the non-perception of subtle objects. (15)
If that which is spatially divided were not considered multiple, but were instead imagined as a single substance, there would be no gradual motion on the earth— meaning there would be no walking—
because the entire distance would be traversed by a single step. Furthermore,
the perception of the near side and the non-perception of the far side could not occur simultaneously.
For it is not logical that the very same thing should, at that time, both be perceived and not perceived.

Furthermore, there could be no occurrence of multiple distinct things, such as elephants, horses, and so forth, in a single location; for if one is exactly where the other is, how can their separation be maintained?
Or how can that [location] be considered one, when it is reached by those two yet not reached by them in the interval between, due to the perception of emptiness therein?
Furthermore, there would be no failure to perceive minute aquatic creatures that possess forms identical to those of larger ones,
if it were assumed that a substance is distinct [from another] solely on account of a difference in characteristics and not otherwise.
Therefore, one must necessarily assume a distinction down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
And that [object] as a single entity is not established;
since it is not established, the fact that form and so forth are the objects of the eye and other [senses] is not established, and thus it is proven that there is representation-only (vijñaptimātra).

Existence or non-existence is determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and among all valid cognitions, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the most authoritative. If the object does not exist, how can this cognition "direct perception" arise? The cognition of direct perception occurs, for example, in dreams and the like.
It has already been made known that [cognition occurs] even without an object;
and when that [cognition] occurs, that object is not being seen—how can its status as a direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) be maintained? (16)
And when that cognition of direct perception occurs— [the thought] "this is my direct perception"— at that time the object is not seen,

because it is determined solely by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and because the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) has already ceased; how, then, can its status as direct perception be maintained?
In particular, since the object is momentary, by that time its form, taste, or whatever else has already ceased.

That which has not been experienced by mental consciousness is not remembered; therefore, there must necessarily have been an experience of the object, and that [experience] is precisely perception (*darśana*). Thus, the claim that the visibility (*pratyakṣatva*) of its objects—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—is established is unproven, because this is merely the recollection of an object already experienced.
For it has been stated how representation (*vijñapti*) appears as that [object].
It has been stated that even in the absence of an external object, a representation such as visual consciousness arises appearing as an object;

from that [representation], recollection follows. For from that very representation, there arises a mental representation associated with memory which conceptualizes form and so forth while appearing as that same object. Thus, the experience of an object is not established by the arising of memory alone.
If, as in a dream, cognition were to have unreal objects as its domain even for one who is awake, then people would themselves realize the non-existence of those objects just as they do in a dream.
But this is not the case;
therefore, it is not true that all perception of objects is devoid of an object, as in a dream.
This is not a proof, because one who has not awakened does not realize the non-existence of the objects seen in a dream. (17)

In this way, the world, asleep through the sleep of the latencies of habitual false conceptualization, perceives unreal objects as if in a dream; not being awakened, it does not correctly understand their non-existence.

But when one becomes awakened through the attainment of supramundane non-conceptual knowledge—which is the antidote to that [sleep]—then, by the manifestation of the pure mundane knowledge obtained subsequent to that [supramundane state], one correctly understands the non-existence of the object. This is the same [as the previous case].
If the representations of sentient beings that appear as objects arise solely from a specific transformation within their own mental continua and not from the specific nature of external objects,

then how is this restriction of representations among sentient beings— resulting from contact with evil or virtuous friends and from hearing true or false teachings— established, given the absence of such contact and the teaching thereof?

The restriction of representation through mutual sovereignty occurs among all sentient beings; for, by virtue of the sovereignty of their mutual representations, there is a restriction of representation among one another as appropriate.
"Mutually" means from one another.
Therefore, a specific representation arises in one mental continuum from a specific representation in another mental continuum, and not from a specific external object.

If, as in a dream, representation were devoid of an object even for one who is awake, why would the practice of wholesome or unwholesome deeds not produce an equal result—desirable or undesirable—in the future for both those who are asleep and those who are awake? [This is] because:
The mind is overcome by torpor during sleep; therefore, the fruit [of an action] therein is not equal [to that of an action performed while awake]. // 18 //
This is the reason here, but not the actual existence of the object.
If this is indeed representation-only, then no one possesses a body or speech.
How does the death of sheep and other animals come about when they are being attacked by slaughterers and the like?
Or, if their death were not caused by those [slaughterers], how could the slaughterers and others be connected with the fault of taking life?

Death is a transformation resulting from a particular representation of another, just as the loss of memory and so forth occurs in others through the power of the minds of beings such as piśācas. (19)

For just as through the power of the minds of piśācas and others, there occur in others disturbances such as loss of memory, seeing dreams, and possession by spirits; and through the power of the mind of one possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhivat*),
just as Sāraṇa had a vision in a dream due to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the noble Mahākātyāyana.
And from the mental malice of the forest-dwelling sages came the defeat of Vemacitra.

Thus, it should be understood that through the sovereign influence of a particular representation of another, a certain transformation arises in others that is antagonistic to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), by which death—defined as the interruption of the homogeneous continuum (*sabhāga-saṃtati*)—occurs.
Or else, how did the Daṇḍaka forest become empty through the anger of the sages?
If it is not accepted that the death of sentient beings occurs through the sovereign influence of a particular representation of another, then consider this:
while the Blessed One was establishing that the punishment of the mind (*manodaṇḍa*) is the most blameworthy, he questioned the householder Upāli:
"Have you heard, householder, by whom were those Daṇḍaka forests, Mātaṅga forests, and Kaliṅga forests emptied and turned into desolate wildernesses?"
He said:
"I have heard, O Gautama, that it was through the mental malice of the sages. How then is it established by him that the punishment of the mind is a great transgression? (20)
If it is imagined that the beings dwelling there were destroyed by non-human beings who were devoted to those [sages], and did not die due to the mental malice of the rishis,
then how, in that case, is it established that the punishment of the mind is the most blameworthy of all, surpassing the punishments of body and speech?
It is established by the mere fact that those beings die through the corruption of his mind alone.
If all this is indeed representation-only, do those who know the minds of others know the minds of others or not?
And what follows from this?
If they do not know them, how can they be known as "knowers of others' minds"?
Now, if they do know [others],
how is it that the knowledge of those who know the minds of others is not in accordance with reality,
whereas their knowledge of their own minds is?
How, then, is that also not in accordance with reality? Because of ignorance, it is not as it is within the range of a Buddha. // 21 //

Just as that [object] is the domain of the Buddhas by way of its ineffable nature, so too, due to ignorance of it, both [subject and object] are not as they truly are; because the false appearance persists, the conceptual construction of grasped and grasper has not been abandoned.
This *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* has been composed by me according to my own capacity, concerning the profundity of the various classifications of the infinite certainty of representation-only; it is,
however, entirely beyond the scope of thought.

However, that [reality] in all its aspects cannot be conceived by those such as myself, because it is beyond the scope of ratiocination (*tarka*). To whom, then, is it the object in every respect? He says:
The sphere of the Buddha. // 22 //
For that is the sphere of all the Blessed Buddhas in every respect, because their knowledge of all objects of knowledge in all their aspects is unimpeded.
The Twenty Verses on the Proof of Cognition-Only.
This is the work of the Master Vasubandhu.
